articles.title: The Odyssey and Spider-Man propel record-breaking summer box office worldwide
articles.summary: The biggest May to September of all time was recorded in US cinemas, with the UK enjoying a 56% rise in audiences, outstripped by an 88% lift in the Middle East and Africa.
body: As well as celebrating their wedding, the actors Tom Holland and Zendaya have something else to toast: their two summer blockbusters – The Odyssey and Spider-Man: Brand New Day – have officially made box office history.
The films were credited as the driving force behind the US’s biggest summer season of all time, taking $4.761bn (£3.51bn) from 1 May-7 September, beating 2013’s $4.756bn.

Spider-Man is currently on $2.4bn worldwide and likely to climb higher, while The Odyssey has made $1.6bn. Other key titles driving sales include Toy Story 5, Michael and The Super Mario Galaxy Movie, all of which have grossed over $1bn.

The breadth of the success of Destin Daniel Cretton’s Spider-Man: Brand New Day was a particular surprise. The film is the best-performing of the year so far and the third highest-grossing film of all time. Its opening weekend was the second-best of all time behind Avengers: Endgame (2019) and it is also the second-fastest film to gross $1bn, doing so in six days.

body: Kidman’s and Bullock’s characters marvel at the naked 6-foot-5 Pace, and a rollicking comic set-piece begins, as they use their powers to bring him to life. Pace, who’d been cast over Zoom and arrived on set only days before, was suddenly thrashing about nude with two actresses he’d adored from afar — forcing himself to be in the moment despite it all. His eyes were meant to be closed, but, Pace says, “it was impossible not to peek a little bit.”

Pace is at once wildly prolific — especially lately — and surprisingly unjaded. When he’s discussing “Practical Magic 2,” he seems like a fan as much as an actor. It’s an almost distant memory though: He is meeting up with me in New York in mid-July on a dayslong break between shoots in Prague and New Zealand, having just wrapped Season 4 of Apple TV’s science fiction saga “Foundation,” in which he’s played a succession of powerful, interrelated characters. He’s about to start the next “Lord of the Rings” sequel, 2027’s Andy Serkis-directed “The Hunt for Gollum,” where he’s reprising his role as elf-king Thranduil.

articles.title: Amalie Næsby Fick on Toronto-Bound ‘What Lies Between Us’ and Challenging Viewers: Would You Defend Your Child, No Matter What? (EXCLUSIVE)
articles.summary: Variety has been given exclusive access “What Lies Between Us” (“Dobbeltfejl”), selected for Toronto’s Discovery section and one of three short-listed Danish pics to become Denmark’s Oscar entry.
body: When producer Louise Vesth first approached Fick with a possible adaptation of the yet-to-be published book “Dobbelfejl” by author Anne Mette Kirk in 2023, she jumped on the offer. As a mother of a young boy, she immediately related to the core of the story – would you defend your child-no matter what?
“I read the book which was a true page-turner, and told Louise I’d love to do a screen adaptation and use the interesting premise as a thriller engine in the film,” Fick tells Variety.
Eager to make the material hers, the helmer had the idea of focusing on Anne Sofie, the mother with the most questionable behaviour, morally and ethically.

“I felt Anne Sofie has the most interesting journey,” says Fick who was keen to explore how her determination to protect her son, no matter what, affects her judgment and her own behaviour. “In all my films and series, I’m interested in characters doing the wrong things, yet we still root for them.”

articles.title: Two times a charm: Is Sandra Bullock and Nicole Kidman’s agelessness the real trick of Practical Magic 2?
articles.summary: A film about sisterhood with fifty- and sixtysomething female leads is something to cheer – but would it have been made if its stars had aged like mere mortals since the 1998 original?
body: Would Hollywood have brought Practical Magic back from the dead if the intervening 28 years looked more visible on Sandra Bullock and Nicole Kidman? An awkward question, as it risks subjecting their faces to the invasive scrutiny older female actors already endure. Their return as leads in their late 50s and early 60s should count as progress. Yet it reveals a condition of female stardom: age can increase a female actor’s nostalgic value, provided it does not show too clearly on her face.

In Practical Magic 2, Bullock, 62, and Kidman, 59, return as sisters Sally and Gillian Owens. Dianne Wiest, 78, and Stockard Channing, 82, are back too. Joey King and Maisie Williams play Sally’s adult daughters, but Sally and Gillian remain central.

As producers, Bullock and Kidman helped choose director Susanne Bier and protect the original’s tone. That creative influence is quite a reversal from 1998, when the film’s female cast and subject matter drew condescension. Bullock remembers being asked: “How many women do you need in a film?” Yet it became a cult favourite. The female world once dismissed as excessive became the source of its value.

articles.title: Alex Winter: ‘Michael Winner was the most erudite sociopath I’ve ever met’
articles.summary: The Bill & Ted actor answers your questions about working with Keanu Reeves, whether there will be a fourth instalment and nights out in Brixton with the Death Wish director. You were born in London but grew up in America. When do you feel most British?
body: My kids ( six and nine) have just discovered Ben 10 in all its incarnations and I saw you directed the live-action versions. If you could choose the powers of any of the aliens in the Omnitrix, which would it be and why? LethalLiaison Heatblast was my favourite. He’s a powerful fire character. My children were obsessed with Ben 10 at the time, and we worked on those together, which was something I don’t often get to do, so it was a lovely experience. I met my wife on that project too. She was running Cartoon Network studios at the time.

Michael Winner directed you in your first film, Death Wish 3. Say something nice about him – and where did you go out drinking when you were filming it in London? ExFi and OttoMaddox I can absolutely say something nice about Michael Winner. He was the most erudite sociopath I’ve ever met. That’s a compliment. We used to drink in Brixton, largely. One of the people working on the show – I think he may have been involved in some criminal activity, so maybe the less said about him the better – owned a club there. They would close it and we would hang out there all night. I was 19 when I made Death Wish 3. It was a very fun, formidable summer.

articles.title: New Strictly hosts explain their roles as they reject 'roving presenter' reports
articles.summary: Johannes Radebe, Josh Widdicombe and Emma Willis say their roles are not "fixed" or defined.
body: Emma Willis, Josh Widdicombe and Johannes Radebe have said they will not have "fixed roles" on Strictly Come Dancing, as they prepare to replace Tess Daly and Claudia Winkleman later this month.
Daly and Winkleman left the programme together at the end of the 2025 series.
Daly was the host on the dancefloor, introducing the dancers and judges, while Winkleman did the post-dance debrief upstairs in the "Clauditorium".
"No one's replacing anybody - at the minute it's all very kind of open," Willis told Richard Osman on The Rest is Entertainment podcast.

articles.title: Pressure review – stormy weather in tense D-day forecast retelling
articles.summary: Andrew Scott finds levels of complexity in a stoic character based on meteorologist James Stagg, the man who persuaded Eisenhower to delay Operation Overlord, for this slick wartime drama.
body: This is to the rage of Col Irving P Krick (Chris Messina), the swaggeringly gung-ho American meteorologist who has always had Ike’s confidence until now. And if we were unsure about this character’s brash-Yank status, in his opening scene he literally shimmies and bops to the Andrews Sisters’ Boogie-Woogie Bugle Boy in the operations room to the uptight, thin-lipped astonishment of Stagg who, as overall commanding officer, tells the Americans to get that piano out of there.

Krick figures they’re good to go on the 5 June, and Stagg’s obduracy also enrages the drawlingly contemptuous General Montgomery (Damien Lewis), who is mustard keen to get boots on the beach pronto. Everyone thinks they need to move right now. Stagg thinks they need to wait. But if he’s wrong, tens of thousands of personnel will die. And to top it off, his wife back in London is nine months pregnant. Pressure fronts of all sorts are closing in.

articles.title: Harry Styles extends tour, with Kylie as a support act
articles.summary: The pop star will play 25 more dates on his Together, Together tour, including three in the London.
body: Harry Styles is extending his record-breaking Together, Together tour in 2027, with 25 more shows, including a return to Wembley Stadium next August.

The singer, who is currently in the middle of a 30-show residency at New York's Madison Square Garden, is adding dates in Ireland, Spain, Italy, Germany and France - who all missed out on the tour's first leg this summer.
Every city will see a different support act, with 80s pop icons Tears For Fears playing at Wembley, and pop legend Kylie Minogue on the bill in Los Angeles.
Although Minogue is a festival headliner in Europe, these shows will represent her first ever stadium concerts in the US.

articles.title: ‘NAZA’ Review: A Sober and Indispensable Doc Highlights the Immoral, State-of-the-Art Killing Machine Employed by the IDF in Gaza
articles.summary: The Guardian served as producer, and Jonathan Glazer as executive producer, on this exposé by Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, part of the directing team behind 2024 Oscar winner 'No Other Land.'
body: It’s hard to describe all of the feelings provoked by watching a film like Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor’s NAZA. Outrage for sure. Indignity as well. Most certainly disgust, on a profound level, for the current Israeli regime and its prime minister, Bibi Netanyahu.

That’s clearly not the purpose of this brave and indispensable movie, which deserves to enter the historical record in the same way as Claude Lanzmann’s Shoah, an excerpt of which we see playing on a screen outside the Tel Aviv Cinematheque. Both works bear witness to acts of genocide — this is the term employed by an IDF officer in the film — and both use a rigorous interview process to get people to speak of the unspeakable, the main difference being that NAZA focuses exclusively on the perpetrators instead of the victims.
